title: Selfishness and Love in Objectivistic Perspective
summary: An essay that I have written for my philosophy assignment during college

blocks.value: SELFISHNESS AND LOVE IN OBJECTIVISTIC PERSPECTIVE
"More than anything else, men and women seek happiness." - Aristotle
I. ABSTRACT

The world sees selfishness as inhumane and considers a selfish person a brute who has no morals and acts only for the immediate gratification of his desires. Altruism therefore treats selfishness as a synonym for evil. To love is one of the innate qualities of man, with happiness as his ultimate goal. "The Salvation of Man is through Love and in Love." This being said, loving others and being selfish seem to contradict man's greatest aspirations.
The text introduces objectivism, defines selfishness, and then discusses the relationship between love, kindness, and selfishness with respect to objectivist principles.
II. OBJECTIVISM IN A NUTSHELL

"My philosophy, in essence, is the concept of man as a heroic being, with his own happiness as the moral purpose of his life, with productive achievement as his noblest activity, and reason as his only absolute." - Ayn Rand
Objectivism is a school of thought developed by Ayn Rand and described by her as a philosophy for living on earth.

Core ideas include: (1) objective reality exists independent of feelings, (2) reason is the only means of perceiving reality and guiding action, (3) rational self-interest and personal happiness are moral purposes, and (4) laissez-faire capitalism is the ideal political-economic system based on voluntary exchange.
III. DEFINING THE WORD SELFISHNESS
"Altruism permits no concept of a self-respecting, self-supporting man..." - Ayn Rand, The Virtue of Selfishness

While altruistic framing often treats selfishness as evil, dictionary meaning centers on concern for one's own interests. The argument here is that selfishness is not unrestrained impulse; it must align with rational moral values. Productive and ethical pursuit of one's interests differs from destructive violation of others.

A thief's evil lies not in pursuing interests but in choosing immoral values that deprive others of happiness. Through an objectivist lens, selfishness is treated as a conjunction of rational and ethical egoism.
IV. LOVE, SELFISHNESS AND OBJECTIVISM
"To love is to value. Only a rationally selfish man, a man of self-esteem, is capable of love..." - Ayn Rand, The Virtue of Selfishness

The essay argues that admiration, respect, friendship, and love arise as emotional responses to values in others. In this view, love is connected to personal happiness and value hierarchies rather than sacrifice for its own sake.
Sacrifice is defined as surrendering a higher value for a lower value or for something one does not value. Rational action, instead, follows value hierarchy.
Example: a husband spending wealth to save his dying wife is not treated as sacrifice if her survival is his highest value. Choosing otherwise against his values would constitute sacrifice.

The essay further discusses parental love, adoption, loyalty, integrity in relationships, and how rational self-interest must remain bounded by moral consistency and non-betrayal of one's core values.
V. KINDNESS, SELFISHNESS AND OBJECTIVISM
Helping others should be guided by value hierarchy, opportunity cost, and risk relative to one's own life and happiness.
The text argues that risking life for a stranger is generally irrational when compared to preserving one's own life, while risking for loved ones may align with deeply held values.
Acts of service by doctors and health workers are interpreted as commitments to professional values, integrity, and oath-based duty rather than mere selfless erasure.
VI. CONCLUSION

The conclusion frames selfishness not as controlling others, but as living according to one's rational values. In this framing, rational and moral self-interest is considered compatible with virtue, happiness, and social progress.
